## Cheat sheet (90 seconds)

| Task | R (stringr/lubridate/forcats) | Python |
|---|---|---|
| contains pattern | `str_detect(x, "ATG")` | `"ATG" in s`, `s.str.contains` |
| extract match | `str_extract(x, "\\d+")` | `re.search(r"\d+", s)` |
| replace | `str_replace(x, " ", "_")` | `s.replace(" ", "_")` |
| case | `str_to_lower(x)` | `s.lower()` |
| trim | `str_trim(x)` | `s.strip()` |
| split | `str_split(x, ",")` | `s.split(",")` |
| join | `paste(x, y, sep = "_")` | `f"{x}_{y}"` |
| parse date | `ymd("2024-03-01")`, `mdy()`, `dmy()` | `pd.to_datetime(..., format=...)` |
| date parts | `year(d)`, `month(d)`, `wday(d)` | `d.year`, `d.month`, `d.dayofweek` |
| floor to week | `floor_date(d, "week")` | `d.to_period("W")` |
| category | `factor(x)`, `fct_reorder()` | `astype("category")` |
| lump rare levels | `fct_lump(n = 5)` | `.value_counts()` + manual |

## Strings: the parsing toolkit

Text cleaning is 90% of "data cleaning", and it's the same four moves every
time: **trim → normalize case → unify separators → extract**. Watch the
pipeline on a typical bioinformatics mess (sample sheet IDs):

```{webr}
#| label: strings
library(stringr)

ids <- c(" sample_038 ", "SAMPLE-42", "sample_7")

str_trim(ids)                       # kill outer whitespace
str_to_lower(str_trim(ids))         # normalize case
str_replace_all(ids, "-", "_")      # unify separators
str_detect(ids, "\\d{2}")           # contains a 2-digit number?
str_extract(ids, "\\d+")            # pull the number out
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: strings-py
import re
ids = [" sample_038 ", "SAMPLE-42", "sample_7"]

print([s.strip() for s in ids])
print([s.strip().lower() for s in ids])
print([s.replace("-", "_") for s in ids])
print([bool(re.search(r"\d{2}", s)) for s in ids])
print([re.search(r"\d+", s).group() for s in ids])
```

The full tidy workflow composes into one pipe — this exact pattern will be
your Project 1 step 2:

```{webr}
#| label: tidy-pipe
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

tibble(raw_id = c(" sample_038 ", "SAMPLE-42", "sample_7")) |>
  mutate(id = str_to_lower(str_trim(raw_id)),
         id = str_replace_all(id, "-", "_"),
         num  = as.numeric(str_extract(id, "\\d+")))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Regex is a transfer skill
`\d`, `+`, `^`, `$`, `[abc]` mean the same in R, Python, grep, and sed.
Learn once, use everywhere. Note R strings need **double backslashes**
(`"\\d"`) — a top-3 source of AI-generated R bugs.
:::

## Factors: categorical memory

Why do factors exist? Three real reasons: **storage** (integers + a lookup
table, which mattered when RAM cost a house), **modeling** (contrast
coding uses the levels), and **plot order** (ggplot2 draws factor levels in
level order, not alphabetical accident). The first reason is history; the
other two are why they're still everywhere — including in sequencing
metadata (batch, condition, cell type).

```{webr}
#| label: factors
library(forcats)

treat <- factor(c("ctrl", "treated", "treated", "ctrl"),
                levels = c("ctrl", "treated"))
as.integer(treat)                 # the codes underneath
levels(treat)                     # the level table

g <- fct_reorder(c("low", "mid", "low", "high"), c(1, 5, 2, 9))
levels(g)                         # reordered by companion values
fct_lump(c(rep("A", 10), "B", "C", "D"), n = 1)  # rare levels -> "Other"
fct_recode(treat, control = "ctrl")   # rename a level (new = old!)
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: factors-py
import pandas as pd
treat = pd.Categorical(["ctrl", "treated", "treated", "ctrl"],
                       categories=["ctrl", "treated"])
print(treat.codes)          # the codes underneath
print(treat.categories)     # the level table
print(pd.Series(treat).cat.rename_categories({"ctrl": "control"}))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The golden rule of factors
**Recode the *values* first, convert to factor last.** If you factorize
first, any spelling variant you missed becomes a level you didn't plan for —
or worse, becomes `NA` when you set explicit levels. You will *see* this
happen in Project 1 if you skip the recode.
:::

## Dates: three formats, one column

The project file mixes `2024-03-01`, `03/10/2024`, and `March 11, 2024`.
In R you'd parse with `parse_date_time(orders = ...)`. Python's
`pd.to_datetime(format="mixed")` (pandas ≥ 2.0) does the same job:

```{pyodide}
#| label: dates-mixed-py
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(["2024-03-01", "03/10/2024", "March 11, 2024"])
print(pd.to_datetime(s, format="mixed"))
```

And the point of parsing is arithmetic — durations, floors, weekday rolls:

```{webr}
#| label: dates
library(lubridate)

d1 <- ymd("2024-03-01")
d2 <- dmy("14/03/2024")

d2 - d1                          # a difftime: 13 days
wday(d2, label = TRUE)           # weekday, spelled out
floor_date(d2, "week")           # rolls back to Sunday
seq(d1, by = "week", length.out = 3)   # a date sequence
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: dates-py
from datetime import date, timedelta
d1 = date(2024, 3, 1)
d2 = date(2024, 3, 14)
print((d2 - d1).days)            # 13
print(d2.strftime("%A"))         # 'Thursday'
print(d1 + timedelta(weeks=2))   # 2024-03-15
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## 03/10 — March 10 or October 3?
Mixed day-first/month-first data is a silent-corruption hazard. Always print
`min()` and `max()` after parsing; if the range looks impossible, your
format guess was wrong.
:::

## Read & refactor: the week's AI-code smells

```r
# ❌ Before
data <- read.csv("raw.csv")
data$date <- as.POSIXct(data$date, format="%m/%d/%Y")  # crashes on the other 2 formats
data$treatment <- ifelse(data$treatment=="control","control", ifelse(data$treatment=="CTRL","control", data$treatment))
data$conc <- as.numeric(gsub("n/a","", data$conc))     # turns "" into NA, but -999 stays!
write.csv(data, "clean.csv", row.names=FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Smell checklist
1. **One format hardcoded** → mixed-format parsing (`parse_date_time` / `format="mixed"`)
2. **Nested ifelse for recodes** → `case_match` / `.replace()`
3. **Sentinels ignored** (`-999`) → `na_if()` / `replace()` BEFORE arithmetic
4. **No guards, no row counts** → assert results, report before/after
5. `gsub("n/a", ...)` as an NA-maker → say what you mean: `na_if()`
:::

## Drills (live pad)

```{webr}
#| label: drills
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)
library(forcats)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

peptides <- c("AngII", "substance P", "BRADYKININ", "AngII")

# 1. Normalize peptides: trim, lower — predict the vector first

# 2. Extract the digits from c("batch1_v2", "batch12_v1", "batch3")

# 3. Which peptides contain "ang" ignoring case? (one call)

# 4. Paste sample and peptide into "sample1-AngII" style IDs (paste or sprintf)

# 5. Parse c("2024-03-01", "01-04-2024") — why does ymd() fail on the second?

# 6. Days from today until 2026-12-31

# 7. What weekday is 2024-02-29? (trick question - check!)

# 8. fct_infreq(peptides): what order do the levels come out in?

# 9. Make a factor with levels in order of appearance (fct_inorder)

# 10. Convert "no", "yes", "yes" to a factor with levels no < yes, then
#     as.numeric() it — what do you get?

# 11. str_sub("ATGGCCATA", 1, 3) — codon extraction; now the last 3

# 12. How many chars in each of c("ATG", "ATGGCC", "")? — one call, integers
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers
1. `str_to_lower(str_trim(peptides))` — "angii" "substance p" "bradykinin" "angii"
2. `str_extract(c("batch1_v2","batch12_v1","batch3"), "\\d+")` — "1" "12" "3"
3. `str_detect(peptides, regex("ang", ignore_case = TRUE))` — TRUE,F,F,TRUE
4. `paste("sample1", peptides[1], sep = "-")`
5. `ymd("01-04-2024")` fails/NA — it's day-first; use `dmy()`
6. `as.Date("2026-12-31") - Sys.Date()` — a difftime
7. 2024 IS a leap year — `wday("2024-02-29", label=TRUE)` → "Thu"
8. most frequent first: AngII, then the singletons alphabetically
9. `fct_inorder(peptides)` — AngII, substance P, BRADYKININ
10. `1 2 2` — factor codes are 1-based level indices, not 0/1
11. "ATG" and "ATA" — str_sub handles start>0, and negative end = from tail
12. `str_length(c("ATG","ATGGCC",""))` — 3, 6, 0
:::

## Python drills (live pad)

```{pyodide}
#| label: drills-py
import re
import pandas as pd

peptides = ["AngII", "substance P", "BRADYKININ", "AngII"]

# 1. Normalize: strip + lower — list comprehension

# 2. Which peptides contain "ang" ignoring case? (one comprehension)

# 3. Extract the digits from c("batch1_v2", "batch12_v1") — re.search

# 4. pd.Series(["no", "yes", "yes"]).astype("category") — print .cat.categories

# 5. Parse ["03/10/2024", "03/15/2024"] to datetime with an explicit format
#    string (hint: %m/%d/%Y)

# 6. (date(2026, 12, 31) - date.today()).days — how many days left in 2026?
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers (Python)
1. `[p.strip().lower() for p in peptides]`
2. `["ang" in p.lower() for p in peptides]` — or `re` with `re.I`
3. `[re.search(r"\d+", s).group() for s in ["batch1_v2", "batch12_v1"]]` — "1", "12"
4. `Index(['no', 'yes'], dtype='object')` — same level table concept as R
5. `pd.to_datetime(..., format="%m/%d/%Y")` — explicit beats guessing
6. A shrinking number — dates are just integers with a costume on
:::

## 🧪 Project 1 — Clean the peptide assay

Files live in `projects/p1/`. **Do it in BOTH languages** — the fix is that
the two pipelines end in the *same numbers*.

**The mess** (`data/peptides_assay.csv`, 125 rows):

- headers with spaces, caps and symbols (` Sample ID `, `Concentration (ng/uL)`)
- `Treatment` spelled `control` / `CTRL` / `Control` / `treated` / `Treated`
- sample IDs with padding whitespace and random CAPS
- concentrations: real values + `"n/a"` + `""` + sentinel `-999`
- dates in **three** formats mixed
- 5 rows duplicated wholesale

**Your pipeline** (same steps in R and Python):

1. snake_case the column names
2. trim + lowercase `sample_id`
3. collapse `treatment` variants to `control` / `treated` (beware `ctrl`!)
4. `n/a`, `""`, `-999` → `NA`, concentration → numeric
5. parse the three date formats to one Date column
6. drop exact duplicates (report how many)
7. factors/Categorical with ordered treatment levels
8. save clean CSV
9. **guards + report**: assert no stray whitespace/`-999`/NA-treatments remain,
   print rows before/after, NAs per column, mean concentration by treatment × peptide

**Starters:** `projects/p1/starter.R` and `projects/p1/starter.py` have the
numbered TODOs. Run from repo root:

```bash
Rscript projects/p1/starter.R
python3 projects/p1/starter.py
```

**Check your numbers:** after cleaning you should see exactly **120 rows,
5 duplicates removed, 13 concentration NAs, 0 treatment NAs**, and mean
AngII concentration ≈ 30.1 (control) vs 32.3 (treated).

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Stuck? The two traps everyone hits
1. `CTRL` → lowercased `"ctrl"` is **not** `"control"`. If you map levels
   without recoding, `ctrl` rows silently become NA. Count NAs after recoding!
2. `read_csv()` trims header whitespace for you, but `pd.read_csv` does NOT —
   Python headers still have the stray spaces until you strip them.
:::

Reference solutions (only after an honest attempt):
`projects/p1/solution.R` · `projects/p1/solution.py` — they print identical
results by design.

## Common pitfalls (real ones)

::: {.callout-warning}
## 1. Regex backslashes
In R source, `"\\d+"` is the regex `\d+`. AI-generated code often ships
`"\d+"` — which R reads as `d+` and matches literal "d"s. Python raw strings
(`r"\d+"`) exist precisely to dodge this.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 2. Factorizing before recoding
Set `levels =` too early and misspelled variants become NA with zero
warning. Sequence: trim/lowercase → recode (`case_match`) → *then*
`factor(..., levels = ...)` → `count()` to prove no NAs.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 3. Sentinel `-999` in means
One `-999` drags a mean of 30 down to 4 without any error — `na_if()`
*before* any statistic, every time. This is why the project makes you count
NAs twice: after recode, after parsing.
:::

## Self-quiz — predict the output

```{webr}
#| label: quiz
# Q1: what prints?
str_extract_all("batch7_v3_sample2", "\\d+")[[1]]

# Q2: what prints?
factor(c("b", "a", "b"), levels = c("a", "b")) |> as.numeric()

# Q3: what prints?
as.numeric(factor(c("high", "low", "mid")))   # no levels given!

# Q4: trap — what does this print? (mixing Date and POSIXct)
ymd("2024-03-10") - ymd_hms("2024-03-09 22:00:00")

# Q5: trap — what prints?
x <- c("a", NA, "b")
x == "b"
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Quiz answers
1. `c("7", "3", "2")` — extract_all returns every match as a character vector
2. `2 1 2` — codes follow the LEVELS order (a=1, b=2), not appearance order
3. `1 2 3` — without explicit levels, alphabetical: high=1, low=2, mid=3.
   (This is why unordered factor codes lie about magnitude.)
4. **Not** "26 hours" — mixing `Date` and `POSIXct` dispatches incompatible
   `-` methods and yields garbage (a nonsense Date). Convert first:
   `as_datetime(ymd(...)) - ymd_hms(...)` → `Time difference of 2 hours`.
   One type per column, per script.
5. `FALSE NA TRUE` — ordinary values compare normally, but `NA == "b"` is NA
   and poisons `ifelse`/filters downstream; use `!is.na(x) & x == "b"` when
   NA positions matter
:::
